_: Explore — the scenes the app opens with.
Each one is a real day at a real place with the layers that show it. The
coordinates and dates are taken from NASA Worldview's own curated stories
(nasa-gibs/worldview, config/.../wv.json/stories), so they point at imagery
that exists; the words are ours. `span` is how many degrees of longitude to
fit, so the same tour frames correctly on a phone and on a large monitor.
`date: latest` resolves to the newest whole day in the archive.
`anim` is [from, to, step] and turns the tour into something to press play on.

tours.title: Today, from orbit
tours.blurb: The whole planet as it was this morning — cloud, snow, dust and smoke, in true colour. Three hours old at most.

tours.title: Where it is burning right now
tours.blurb: Every pixel VIIRS found hot enough to be a fire in the last 24 hours, over the picture it took at the same moment.

tours.title: Hurricane Florence, hour by hour
tours.blurb: A category-4 storm filling the western Atlantic, with the rain it was dropping painted over it. Press play and watch it walk into the Carolinas.

tours.title: Dorian stalls over the Bahamas
tours.blurb: One of the strongest Atlantic landfalls ever recorded, sitting still for a day and a half. The eye is the hole you can see the sea through.

tours.title: The Black Summer
tours.blurb: Australia's 2019-20 bushfire season from above: fire detections in red, and the smoke running out over the Tasman Sea.

tours.title: Camp Fire, the morning it started
tours.blurb: 8 November 2018. A plume that reached San Francisco by lunchtime, from a fire you can watch begin at the top of the smoke.

tours.title: The iceberg that left Larsen C
tours.blurb: July 2017: a crack finishes crossing an ice shelf and a berg the size of a small country floats free. The line is 200 km long.

tours.title: The Aral Sea, year by year
tours.blurb: One frame each August from 2000. A sea the size of Ireland becomes a salt desert while you watch — the clearest thing satellite imagery has ever shown.

tours.title: Earth at night
tours.blurb: The VIIRS day-night band is sensitive enough to see a fishing boat's lamps. Cities, gas flares, and the moonlight on the clouds between them.

tours.title: El Niño, as a temperature map
tours.blurb: Sea surface temperature anomalies across the Pacific in late 2023 — how far each patch of ocean is from its own normal for that week.

tours.title: Saharan dust crossing an ocean
tours.blurb: June 2020: a plume big enough to be named crosses the Atlantic and reaches the Caribbean. True colour, with aerosol depth on top.

tours.title: Sinabung erupts
tours.blurb: 19 February 2018. An ash column punching through the cloud deck over Sumatra, seen from 700 km up.

tours.title: Sunglint
tours.blurb: When the sea reflects the sun straight back at the sensor, the ocean turns to hammered metal and every current and slick shows up in it.

tours.title: Snow in southern Africa
tours.blurb: August 2018, and the Drakensberg is white. A reminder that the map is not a picture of the usual — it is a picture of that day.
